# Graphing in Excel {#sec-graphing-excel}

Excel builds a chart from cells. The work therefore begins with the table: decide what one row represents, calculate the values needed for the comparison and check that the chart reads the intended columns.

This chapter uses two datasets. [`field_yields.csv`](practice/data/field_yields.csv) contains sixty simulated canola fields. [`rm_yields_2015_2024.csv`](practice/data/rm_yields_2015_2024.csv) contains published Saskatchewan RM crop yields. The Excel and R chapters answer the same four questions so that the software does not change the analysis.

## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

::: {.objectives}
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Arrange a worksheet table for a bar, line, scatter or histogram chart.
2. Choose the chart type that fits a comparison, trend, relationship or distribution.
3. Check the source range, number of plotted observations and category order.
4. Add descriptive labels and units without repeating information.
5. Set an axis range that represents the comparison honestly.
6. Copy a finished chart into a report or save it as an image.
:::

## The worked workbook {#sec-excel-graphing-workbook}

The workbook contains a separate sheet for each chart and keeps the source data on their own sheets. Each chart sheet shows the table that drives the chart, the formulas used to calculate it and a short set of checks.

Open the **README** sheet first. The remaining sheets follow the same sequence as the examples below.

## Compare regional means with bars {#sec-excel-bar-example}

The first question is whether mean field yield differs across the three regions. The chart needs one row per region, not one row per field, so the **Bar chart** sheet calculates the three means with `AVERAGEIF`.

Central averages 47.6 bu/ac, North 47.3 bu/ac and South 42.7 bu/ac. Each mean uses nineteen recorded yields. The Central--North difference is only 0.3 bu/ac, which is small beside the variation among individual fields.

The source table is arranged from highest to lowest and the value axis begins at zero. There is one series, so a legend would repeat information already supplied by the title.

## Show change through time with a line {#sec-excel-line-example}

The **Line chart** sheet averages the available canola yields across RMs for each year from 2015 to 2024. A line is appropriate because the years have a meaningful order and equal spacing.

The lowest annual mean in the series is 21.9 bu/ac in 2021. The chart makes that point easy to find, but the plotted value should still be checked against the formula-driven table. `AVERAGEIF` ignores blank RM yields rather than treating them as zero.

The vertical axis does not begin at zero. A line encodes values by position rather than bar length, so a narrower scale can be used, provided the displayed range does not exaggerate ordinary movement.

## Compare two numeric variables with a scatter plot {#sec-excel-scatter-example}

The **Scatter plot** sheet places field size on the horizontal axis and yield on the vertical axis. This must be an XY scatter chart. A line chart would treat the field sizes as ordered labels and connect observations that do not form a sequence.

Fifty-seven points are plotted because three fields have no recorded yield. The cloud has little visible slope, and the correlation is about -0.07. Field size and yield show almost no linear relationship in these simulated data.

## Show a distribution with a histogram {#sec-excel-histogram-example}

The **Histogram** sheet counts recorded yields in intervals 3 bu/ac wide. Its formulas use a lower bound that is included and an upper bound that is excluded; the last interval includes 63 so that the maximum of 60.7 bu/ac is counted.

The eleven bin counts add to 57, the number of recorded yields. Changing the bin width changes the visible shape, especially with a small dataset, so the chosen width belongs in the chart title or surrounding explanation.

Excel also has a built-in **Histogram** chart under **Insert > Statistical Chart**. The formula-driven version in the workbook makes the bin boundaries and count check visible.

## Titles, axes and legends {#sec-excel-chart-elements}

Use **Chart Design > Add Chart Element** to add or remove titles, axis labels, legends and data labels. A title or axis should state the unit when it is not already clear. `Average field yield by region (bu/ac)` supplies both the comparison and the unit.

Bar charts normally need a zero baseline. Select the value axis, open **Format Axis**, and set its Minimum bound to 0. Mac users use the **Chart Design** tab for chart elements; the `+` button beside a selected chart is Windows-only.

A legend is needed when colour or shape identifies several series. A one-series chart does not need a legend that says `Mean yield`. Data labels are useful when exact values matter and there are few marks; labelling every point in a scatter plot usually covers the pattern.

## Formatting and export {#sec-excel-chart-export}

Remove borders, gridlines or colours that do not help the comparison. Keep light gridlines when readers need to estimate values from an axis. Avoid three-dimensional effects, shadows and patterned fills.

Copying a chart from Excel into Word or PowerPoint provides several paste options. **Picture** or **Paste Special > Picture (PNG)** fixes the appearance and prevents later workbook edits from changing the document. A linked chart updates from the workbook but can break when the files are moved or shared.

Desktop Excel can also use **Save as Picture** from a chart's right-click menu; Excel for the web cannot. Before handing over a chart, compare one plotted value with its source cell and check the category order, axis range, labels, units and number of observations.
